prompt: Explain the difference between tight coupling and loose coupling in software design. Give one example of each in Java.
ground_truth: Tight: a class depends directly on concrete implementation of another (e.g. new ConcreteClass() inside it). Loose: depends on abstractions/interfaces so implementations can be swapped (e.g. constructor-injected interface). Java examples must show this.

prompt: Explain the Dependency Inversion Principle (DIP). Provide a Java example demonstrating how DIP can reduce coupling between two classes.
ground_truth: High-level modules should not depend on low-level modules; both should depend on abstractions. Abstractions should not depend on details. Example must introduce an interface that both sides depend on, with the dependency injected.

prompt: Explain the Liskov Substitution Principle (LSP) using a simple Java example. Also explain what could happen if a subclass violates LSP.
ground_truth: Objects of a subtype must be usable wherever the supertype is expected without breaking program correctness (Barbara Liskov). Violations cause broken client assumptions, unexpected exceptions, strengthened preconditions (e.g. Rectangle/Square).

prompt: Explain the Observer design pattern. Describe the relationship between the Subject/Observable and its Observers and explain what happens when the Subject's state changes.
ground_truth: One-to-many dependency. Subject keeps a list of observers; when its state changes it notifies all registered observers automatically (they update themselves). Promotes loose coupling.

prompt: What does the Open/Closed Principle mean? Explain how a Java program can be extended without modifying existing source code.
ground_truth: Software entities should be open for extension but closed for modification. In Java: abstractions (interfaces/abstract classes) and polymorphism so new behaviour is added via new classes.

prompt: Explain the Single Responsibility Principle. Give a short Java example of a class that violates it and show how to refactor it.
ground_truth: A class should have only one reason to change (one responsibility/actor). Example must show a class mixing concerns (e.g. logic + persistence + printing) split into separate classes.

prompt: Explain the Interface Segregation Principle with a Java example.
ground_truth: Clients should not be forced to depend on methods they do not use. Prefer several small, client-specific interfaces over one large interface. Example splits a fat interface.

prompt: Explain encapsulation in Java and list the four access modifiers with what each allows.
ground_truth: Encapsulation: bundling data and behaviour and hiding internal state behind a public interface. Access levels: private (same class), default/package-private (same package), protected (package + subclasses), public (everywhere).

prompt: Explain the difference between method overriding and method overloading in Java, with a short example of each.
ground_truth: Overriding: subclass redefines an inherited method with the same signature; resolved at runtime (dynamic dispatch). Overloading: same method name with different parameter lists in the same class; resolved at compile time.

prompt: Explain the differences between an abstract class and an interface in Java (Java 8 or later).
ground_truth: Abstract class: can hold state and constructors, single inheritance of class. Interface: a class can implement many; since Java 8 may have default and static methods; fields are implicitly public static final; no instance state.

prompt: Explain the design guideline 'favour composition over inheritance' and give a Java example of each approach.
ground_truth: Prefer has-a (composition/delegation) to is-a inheritance for flexibility, runtime change of behaviour and to avoid tight coupling/fragile base class. Examples must correctly show both.

prompt: Explain the Factory Method design pattern and give a Java example.
ground_truth: Defines an interface/method for creating an object but lets subclasses decide which concrete class to instantiate, decoupling client from concrete classes.

prompt: Explain the Strategy design pattern and give a Java example.
ground_truth: Defines a family of interchangeable algorithms behind a common interface; the context holds a strategy and it can be swapped at runtime.

prompt: Explain the Singleton pattern and the thread-safety problems of a naive lazy-initialised implementation in Java. Name two ways to make it thread-safe.
ground_truth: Singleton: one instance with global access. Naive lazy init (if instance==null) is not thread-safe (race can create two instances). Fixes: eager init, synchronized getInstance, double-checked locking with volatile, holder idiom, enum singleton (any two).

prompt: In UML class diagrams, explain the difference between association, aggregation and composition.
ground_truth: Association: general 'uses/knows' relationship. Aggregation: whole-part where part can exist independently (hollow diamond). Composition: strong ownership, part's lifetime depends on the whole (filled diamond).

prompt: Explain the Decorator design pattern and name one example from the Java standard library.
ground_truth: Wraps an object implementing the same interface to add behaviour dynamically without changing its class. Library example: java.io streams/readers such as BufferedReader or BufferedInputStream wrapping another stream (also Collections.unmodifiableList-style wrappers).

prompt: Explain the difference between checked and unchecked exceptions in Java and give two examples of each.
ground_truth: Checked: subclasses of Exception excluding RuntimeException; must be caught or declared (e.g. IOException, SQLException). Unchecked: RuntimeException subclasses (and Errors); not enforced (e.g. NullPointerException, IllegalArgumentException).

prompt: Explain the contract between equals() and hashCode() in Java and why both should be overridden together.
ground_truth: If two objects are equal by equals(), they must return the same hashCode(). Violating it breaks hash-based collections (HashMap/HashSet). Unequal objects may share a hash code.

prompt: In the context of software design, explain the meaning of Rigidity, Fragility, Viscosity, and Immobility. Explain how these characteristics contribute to software rot.
ground_truth: Rigidity: hard to change, changes cascade. Fragility: changes break unrelated parts. Immobility: hard to reuse parts elsewhere. Viscosity: easier to hack than to preserve design (design or environment viscosity). Together they signal a rotting design (Robert C. Martin).

prompt: What does the acronym STUPID represent in discussions of poor software design? Explain each characteristic and give an example of one of them in Java.
ground_truth: Singleton, Tight coupling, Untestability, Premature optimization, Indescriptive naming, Duplication.

prompt: Explain the Delegation pattern as described in design-pattern literature. How does delegation differ from inheritance?
ground_truth: An object handles a request by passing it to a helper (delegate) object, reusing behaviour via composition at runtime. Inheritance is a static compile-time is-a relationship.

prompt: What is a Marker Interface in Java? Give two real examples from the Java standard library and explain what purpose they serve.
ground_truth: An interface with no methods that tags a class with a capability. Real examples: java.io.Serializable, java.lang.Cloneable, java.util.RandomAccess, java.util.EventListener. Both named must exist with correct purposes.

prompt: Explain the purpose of Java's Serializable interface. Is Serializable a normal interface with methods that a programmer must implement?
ground_truth: Serializable is a marker interface with no methods; it permits object serialization via ObjectOutputStream. serialVersionUID and transient are relevant. Programmer need not implement methods.

prompt: Explain the Law of Demeter and show a Java example of a violation.
ground_truth: Principle of least knowledge: an object should only talk to its immediate collaborators, not to strangers. Violation: long call chains such as a.getB().getC().doX().

prompt: What is the Hollywood Principle in software design? Give an example of it in practice.
ground_truth: 'Don't call us, we'll call you': high-level framework/component calls low-level components (inversion of control). Examples: Template Method, framework callbacks, event listeners, dependency injection containers.

prompt: What is the 'fragile base class problem' in object-oriented design?
ground_truth: Seemingly safe changes to a base class can break subclasses because of tight coupling via inheritance (e.g. changed self-calls/overridable methods).

prompt: What are covariant return types in Java? Give a short example.
ground_truth: Since Java 5, an overriding method may return a subtype of the return type declared in the overridden method. Example: Animal reproduce() overridden as Dog reproduce().

prompt: What is the 'Feature Envy' code smell? How would you fix it?
ground_truth: A method that uses data/methods of another class more than its own (Fowler, Refactoring). Fix: Move Method to the class whose data it uses.
